claims.claim: A return is the gain or loss on an investment over a period of time, typically expressed as a percentage; a positive return is a gain and a negative return is a loss.
The simple (holding period) return is calculated as (ending value − starting value) ÷ starting value; expressing returns in percentage terms allows investments of different sizes to be compared.

A total return has two building blocks: income received while holding the investment (dividends or interest) and the change in the investment's price; a price increase is a capital gain and a price decrease is a capital loss.
The realized return of an investment is the total return that actually occurs over a particular time period, measured after the fact.

The expected return is what an investor anticipates before the outcome: the expected value of the distribution of possible returns; it is based on historical data, which may or may not reliably forecast future returns, so the outcome is not guaranteed.

Higher expected returns come with higher risk: as investment risks rise, investors seek higher returns to compensate themselves for taking such risks; investors require a higher expected return for riskier investments.
Returns are compared across investments in percentage terms, and across different holding periods on an annualized (per-year) basis so the comparison is fair.

Past returns are history, not promises: expected return is based on historical data that may not reliably forecast future returns, the outcome is not guaranteed, and all investments involve some degree of risk.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources frame return differently: CFI and Investopedia define it as the money made or lost over a period (which can be negative), while OpenStax describes return as the benefit, or profit, the investor expects from an expenditure (forward-looking).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats the framings as complementary: the working definition follows CFI/Investopedia (gain or loss over a period, positive or negative), and OpenStax's 'benefit the investor expects' is presented as the expectation side of the story, with the realized return as the after-the-fact measurement.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Finance, Section 15.1: Risk and Return to an Individual Asset
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook; aiIngestionAllowed:false per subject source-map, so read via Internet Archive capture dated 2023 and restated). Supports: risk and return as 'the two Rs of finance'; return as the benefit, or profit, the investor expects from an expenditure; the realized return as the total return that occurs over a particular time period; total dollar return = dividend income + capital gain; capital gain and capital loss; holding-period percentage return = (ending − starting)/starting (example: $228.50 share sold at $261.90 returns 14.62%); percentage returns as the basis for comparing investments of different sizes; annualizing a holding-period return to an effective annual rate so different holding periods can be compared; volatility of returns as risk. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Rate of Return (Corporate Finance Institute)

Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Return: What It Means in Investing, How It Is Measured
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary; JS-walled live, so verified via Internet Archive snapshot 2024-06-01 of the 2023-updated article).
